Chapter 31

The jam room

A load that makes a missing room a real 404, params as a typed prop, and the live query on screen: $derived(await room) so the page follows every yield, overridable {let} deriveds for knobs in mid-gesture, room.connected and reconnect(), online from the window, presence with animate:flip, a handle form that carries the room id, and every edit as a command — with the server’s reason when one is refused.

By the end of this chapter

Consume a query.live correctly — including the mistake that shows the first snapshot forever — and let a person edit a value that the server also updates, without the two fighting.

Before the room, one question: does it exist? The live room is awaited further down inside a boundary with a pending snippet, and on the server a boundary like that renders only its pending snippet — so the server never opens the stream, and could not know that /jam/nowhere names nothing. It used to answer 200 with “Joining the room…”, and the browser found out after hydration. A *soft 404* like that is wrong for anything that reads statuses: a link checker, a crawler, a chat app drawing a preview. So a universal load awaits getRoomName(params.room), a plain query that throws error(404, "No such room") (ch. 25). On the server it runs before anything renders, so the response is a real 404 with the error page; on a client-side navigation it runs in the browser, and the same error page is drawn without a document load. The name it returns is the page’s <title>.

params comes in as a prop, typed by the generated PageProps as { room: string }, beside the data the load returned. watchRoom(id) is the live query from chapter 25. Awaiting it gives the current room; after that, its value updates every time the server yields. room.connected says whether the stream is up, and room.reconnect() restarts it by hand — SvelteKit reconnects on its own with backoff, and eagerly when the browser comes back online.

The comment in the file is the whole chapter in three sentences. A declaration tag with a plain await runs *once* — it is a blocking promise, not a subscription — and would show the first snapshot forever, while the server yields to nobody. Wrapping it in $derived is what makes it re-run every time the live query yields: the resource’s then is reactive, and a derived is what tracks it. This cost an afternoon and two end-to-end tests, and it is the reason every await in this project’s markup that should follow its inputs is written $derived(await …).

Why {let bpm = $derived(...)}

The tempo knob has two writers: the person turning it, and the room’s next snapshot. An *overridable derived* — let rather than const — follows the room and can be assigned by the knob while a gesture is in progress. When the next snapshot arrives the derived recomputes and the override is gone, replaced by whatever the server settled on, which is usually the same number. Neither writer needs to know about the other.

Presence is the present array from the snapshot: every open stream, by handle. Keyed by id with animate:flip and a scale transition, so a person joining slides into place and a person leaving shrinks away — unless they asked for reduced motion, which is what the two durations at the top of the script ask for each time (ch. 30 says why a Svelte transition has to ask). online from svelte/reactivity/window is navigator.onLine as a reactive value, and the chip says so before the stream has noticed.

A browser with no handle sees a form. It carries the room id as a hidden field, and the handler (ch. 24) calls watchRoom(room).reconnect() so that the stream — which read the cookie when it opened — restarts and shows the new name in the presence list. The same whoAmI() query the header reads is read here, and the form’s refresh() updates both.

The grid is the studio’s StepGrid with tools={false} — no per-track buttons, because tracks are shared — and every callback is a command. onpaint reads the current step from the snapshot, computes the next velocity with the same cycleVelocity the studio uses, and sends a Step with a real Note in it; the transport hook (ch. 26) carries it across. Nothing is changed locally: the room’s next yield is what redraws the pad, for this browser and every other.

Every chip and every preset button goes through run, at the top of the file. A command the server refuses — a mute for a track that a preset loaded in another browser has just replaced — rejects with an HttpError, and run puts its body.message in a toast: “No such track in this room”. Before messageOf (ch. 24) it read (e as Error).message, which on an HttpError is undefined, and every refused edit produced an empty toast.

Why the failed snippet reads error.message and run does not

They are handed different things. Whatever the stream fails with — a server that has stopped answering, say — the boundary catches it, and SvelteKit runs it through handleError before the snippet sees it. The documentation puts it in a comment on its own example: the error “went through the handleError hook and is of type App.Error” — { status, message }, so error.message is the server’s sentence. The error page that a missing room now lands on is handed the same shape, as its error prop. An awaited command is not inside a boundary at all: its promise rejects with the HttpError itself, { status, body }, and the sentence is one level down. Same server, same error(…) call, two shapes — and a probe that threw both in a browser is how this project found out which code read which. The (error as App.Error) is the documented type in the only place today’s typings let it go (ch. 19).

Checkpoint

  • You can say what would be on screen if {const snapshot = $derived(await room)} lost its $derived.
  • You can explain what happens to a knob override when the next snapshot arrives.
  • You can trace one pad click from this page to every other browser in the room.
  • You can say what a refused command hands run, and what a failed stream hands the failed snippet.
  • You can say why /jam/nowhere needed a load to be a 404, when the live query already threw one.
